Channel 4 boss Priya Dogra has been quizzed by British MPs over the proliferation of sexual abuse scandals currently plaguing the local television industry.

Dogra, who joined Channel 4 last December, was cross-examined at a Department for Culture, Media and Sport meeting Tuesday morning alongside the network's chair Geoff Cooper.

Committee chair Caroline Dinenage opened the meeting with questioning about Brand, saying she had spoken to one of his victims, pseudonymously called "Bella," a former Channel 4 employee. According to Dinenage, Bella complained again in 2023 after Channel 4 broadcast a documentary about Brand as part of the Sunday Times investigation that eventually led to him being charged with multiple counts of abuse. He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual misconduct earlier this month.

"Her complaint was not investigated properly in 2009," Dogra acknowledged. "It should have been. It wasn't escalated properly. Alex [Mahon, Dogra's predecessor at Channel 4] apologized for that. That apology stands, and it shouldn't have happened." She added the network has since strengthened its whistle-blowing protocols.

But Dinenage interrupted to point out that despite her complaint being ignored in 2009, Bella had complained again in 2023 to Channel 4, when the network had pledged to hold an internal investigation into Brand. According to Dinenage, Bella described that inquiry as "shambolic and a whitewash." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"When Bella made her complaints in 2023, again it was not handled properly, and it's almost unforgivable that happened twice," Dogra said, adding shortly after: "I'm not sure we can apologize enough as an organization for putting her through that twice. We have apologized in public in the past and in private."

She noted later during the Q&A session that when Bella originally complained, "There were no findings at that stage of Russell Brand ‘s behavior. There was sort of rumor and speculation, but there was no real finding. That has now changed."

In addition to additional protocols, the CEO said she has also made it mandatory for all production companies Channel 4 works with to sign up to the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority.

Dogra was also quizzed over its hiring practices, given Brand's behavior was overlooked or even enabled by many people in the industry. "In media, we create stars. That's what TV does, that's what film does, and they can appear larger than life," she said. "The backbone of this industry is freelancers, and they generally work on short-term contracts, and that sort of exacerbates, if you will, the power imbalance." She said the network is "creating more resources" for freelancers to help "spot patterns early on."

Dogra also said that "as an industry," networks and companies would need to show "that commercial interests do not override our principles" and that broadcasters would need to be prepared to walk away "from a big show" or a "big personality" because it does not align with its values. "I've had to do that on a recent show," she added, referring to her recent decision to cancel "Married at First Sight U.K." after allegations of sexual abuse were made by some of the contestants.

Asked why she decided to cancel the show following the results of two reviews, commissioned by Channel 4, to determine whether its welfare protocols were adequate, Dogra said "I felt that the wholesale implementation of those recommendations [in the reports] would lead to a completely different show."

She also said she was "uncomfortable" with "some aspects of the recommendations," such as 24/7 recording for monitoring safety and double locking rooms and bathrooms. "I didn't feel that was a show that I wanted to be making," Dogra said, adding the show's "hefty program budget" would be reinvested in new content. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

But she admitted that as one of Channel 4's most popular shows, "Married at First Sight" was "incredibly commercially attractive for us. I'm not going to sugarcoat that."

"It was a very profitable show, and therefore, if it's profitable, it pays for all sorts of other programming…. And so to say that it won't be a loss to the financials would be wrong. Of course, it will."

During the almost two-hour long session, Dogra also noted that, following allegations about comedian David Walliams, who is now being investigated for historic sexual offences, the network had "removed any programs" in which he featured.

articles.title: Fubo Widens Quarterly Loss on Higher Revenue, Gets to 5.75 Million North America Subscribers
articles.summary: The sports-focused streamer unveiled moves after merging with Walt Disney’s Hulu+ live TV business and under new CEO Alisa Bowen.
articles.content:
Fubo TV widened its fourth quarter loss on higher revenue and got to 5.75 million North American subscribers after merging with Walt Disney 's Hulu + live TV business.

Fubo had 6 million North American subscribers in the prior-year fourth quarter. The overall subscriber base now represents customers for Fubo ‘s live TV streaming services, including Fubo and Hulu + Live TV, after closing a merger deal with Disney.

Fubo will no longer report total subscribers starting with the current fiscal year and its first quarter. With the reveal of its latest financial results partly on a pro forma basis after closing Disney's Hulu merger, Fubo ended the fourth quarter with a net loss of $51.8 million, compared to a net loss of $38.8 million in the same period of 2025, and on overall revenue at $1.5 billion, up from a year-earlier $1.48 billion. Adjusted EBITDA was $12.3 million, against a year-earlier $4.1 million on a pro forma basis. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Business Disney Beats Wall Street Expectations as Entertainment and Parks Power Latest Quarter TV Jen Affleck Breaks Free: The 'Mormon Wives' Star on Her Divorce and Finding Herself on the 'Orange County' Spinoff

During the three months to Sept. 30, Fubo TV saw subscription revenue come to $327 million. That compares to a year-earlier $406.8 million in reported subscription revenue, before Fubo gets set to align with Disney's fiscal calendar in the first quarter of 2026.

Advertising revenue edged higher to $119.1 million, against a pro forma advertising revenue of $97.5 million in the prior-year period. With CEO Alisa Bowen now at the helm at Fubo, the company announced the launch of a Disney+ and Hulu (With Ads) bundle for subscribers of Fubo's pro and elite plans at no additional cost starting this week.

"With profitability as its North Star, the company will focus on two core audiences, Fubo's passionate sports fans and the highly engaged general entertainment viewers of Hulu + Live TV, and give both more ways to discover the full range of content available to them," the company said in a statement.

articles.title: 5 Shows That Are Better Than They Should Be Thanks to Their Cast, Including a Series Saved by Netflix
articles.summary: Sometimes you start watching a show and realize the story isn't appealing or, while the writing has its merits, it isn't exactly brilliant overall. This happens more often than you might think, but somehow, you find yourself getting more invested and notice it's mostly because of the characters. Yes, in some cases, the cast is […]
articles.content:
Here is a list of series that were loved by audiences (at least by a large portion of them), and had some questionable quality, failed to live up to their own premises , or featured flaws that were just too hard to overlook, but their casts made everything work.

For a long time, How to Get Away with Murder was a series that kept people hooked, as each season relied on flash-forwards to build suspense. On the other hand, the writing wasn't always as strong as it could have been . It often felt like the show was competing with itself to come up with the next big twist, which worked, but only for so long. The story follows Annalise Keating (Viola Davis), a criminal defense attorney and law professor who selects five students to work with her on real cases. What none of them expects, though, is that this experience will eventually pull all of them into a series of crimes and situations they'll do just about anything to keep hidden.

The plot is then driven by investigations, drama, and conflicts that often put everyone in difficult situations. However, not everything is so convincing, and some moments can feel like too much just for the sake of making an impact. Still, one thing that's hard to deny is that a big reason audiences stuck with it for so long was its cast — especially Davis, who pretty much carried every episode with a performance that was even better than the material called for. Thanks to her bringing so much depth to her character, you might not even remember that How to Get Away with Murder had its weaker moments. But the rest of the cast also deserves credit for making the dynamic between the students intriguing all the time.

In the beginning, The Walking Dead was a worldwide phenomenon, to the point that plenty of people would religiously tune in every Sunday for a new episode . But at some point, the show started losing its way, with behind-the-scenes changes and different directions for the plot that gradually drove more and more fans away over its 11-season run. The story begins with Rick Grimes (Andrew Lincoln), a police officer who wakes up from a coma to discover that the world has been overrun by zombies . And after finding other survivors, he takes on the responsibility of leading the group in search of safety, only to realize that humans can be pretty dangerous and violent as well. And before some of the actors started leaving the show, their performances had already gotten you attached to their characters.

Alongside Lincoln, Norman Reedus and Melissa McBride, as Daryl and Carol, were some of the big standouts from the very start, to the point where you could find yourself caring more about what happened to them than about the overall storyline. The cast was so good that even characters who initially didn't seem to have much to offer got room to develop, and you wanted to see more of them . Plus, you probably had your own favorites, and no matter how many others died, you kept rooting for the ones you cared about. That's what helped keep The Walking Dead going for so long, even as it started to decline because of repetitive drama, stories that dragged on longer than they should have, and the simple fact that zombies took a backseat to human rivalries .

If you watch a few episodes of Suits , you'll realize the show doesn't have a complicated formula. You meet Mike (Patrick J. Adams) , a young man with a photographic memory and a natural talent for law who lands a job at a New York law firm despite never having attended law school. Harvey (Gabriel Macht), the lawyer who decides to hire him, knows about the lie but is willing to take the risk, setting up a partnership that has to remain a secret. And whenever someone threatens to expose the truth, the two spend most of the episode trying to find a way out, only for everything to get resolved before another complication comes along to keep the story moving.

Looking at the series as a whole, it's entertaining, but it relies almost entirely on that formula, which makes the situations too predictable. In theory, it's an idea that only works temporarily, because if Mike's secret ever gets exposed, the dynamic of the show has to change. But even when you notice that, you keep watching, and that's because of the ridiculously charismatic cast — and it's not just the leads. The supporting characters have strong personalities and are always stealing the spotlight, even when professional tensions turn into personal matters. Basically, the whole cast has amazing chemistry. In fact, Suits even gained a bigger following after it ended, which shows just how much people kept enjoying it .

You know what it means to be creative? Once Upon a Time had exactly that going for it with its premise: bringing together famous classic fairy-tale characters in an apparently ordinary town, where they have to deal with problems that are very different from what we'd naturally expect from them. The story begins when Emma Swan (Jennifer Morrison) arrives in Storybrooke and discovers that the town's residents are actually characters whose memories were erased by a curse. Then, the show starts exploring several versions of these stories, introducing new figures that you have known for ages. However, eventually, you really need to be patient with just how much lore the series keeps piling up.

The approach leads to some great moments that keep you invested, especially because the story itself taps into the audience's nostalgia. But the writing can't maintain the same level of quality all the way through, and the special effects don't always help either. Still, if you've watched Once Upon a Time , you probably remember it quite fondly, almost like a comfort show. And do you know why? The cast: it's enormous, but easily the production's biggest achievement, no wonder the Evil Queen (Lana Parrilla) became a fan favorite (Rumplestiltskin (Robert Carlyle) and Captain Hook (Colin O'Donoghue) are other standouts). With so many found-family dynamics between the characters, you get attached to their relationships and care about what happens to them until you find yourself bingeing every episode .

Ask someone what they think of Lucifer , and there's a good chance you'll hear some negative opinions. It's not exactly a show that's well-regarded, even if it's far from terrible. The story revolves around Lucifer Morningstar (Tom Ellis) , the Devil himself, who starts working as a police consultant after meeting Chloe (Lauren German), a detective who seems to be immune to his powers of persuasion. Meanwhile, he also has to deal with problems involving his siblings, his father, and the consequences of letting go of his responsibilities in Hell. The series follows that hybrid structure, with a different case in each episode while a storyline develops alongside it — but that's the main problem.

Shows like The X-Files and House became iconic using that same structure, but they knew how to develop their identities, character arcs, and stories. Lucifer , on the other hand, often relied on the formula and struggled to go beyond the conventional police format, even though its premise had so much potential. Still, you keep watching because of Ellis: much like Davis in How to Get Away with Murder , he has the ability to embody his character on every level, and without his performance, many of the jokes and situations that make the show good wouldn't have the same effect. And even when some of the supporting storylines fall a little flat, the cast does its best to make them more engaging. It's no wonder the show got canceled only to be brought back by Netflix after fans campaigned to save it.

articles.title: Disney Expects to Increase Annual Content Spend to $26 Billion Next Year
articles.summary: The increase in spending is due to more international fare, sports rights, and the timing of feature film production.
articles.content:
The Walt Disney Co. isn't slowing down when it comes to spending major cash on original content.

The company disclosed Tuesday in its quarterly earnings report that it expects to spend $26 billion on content in fiscal 2027 (which started this quarter), up 9 percent from the $24 billion or so it spent in fiscal 2026.

Disney says that the increase in spending is being driven by increased investment in international programming, growing sports rights costs, and the timing of feature film production spend. Related Stories Business Disney Hires Netflix PR Vet Emily Feingold as Comms VP, Replacing David Jefferson Business Bob Iger's New Book to Chronicle "Sometimes Bumpy, Never Boring" Second Stint as Disney CEO

Disney has been pursuing more international programming as it seeks to grow its streaming business abroad, while sports rights like the NBA and NFL continue to rise like clockwork every year. Film production, meanwhile, can be lumpy, with some years with a lot of physical production and other years with less. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For comparison, the newly-formed Skydance is telling Hollywood that it is committing to spend some $30 billion annually on content, inclusive of sports, films and TV, while Netflix is spending $20 billion on content this year. Comcast is in the $25 billion range.

KPMG, in an analysis released last week , noted how more and more professional content spend is being sent toward creators and live sports, a trend that is true for Disney, which has been adding creator content to Disney+, and which continues to bulk up ESPN.

But Disney is also cutting costs, revealing plans to generate $3 billion in run-rate synergies by 2029… with the savings largely being plowed into more content and experiences.

articles.title: These (Alleged) Reality TV Lies From AGT To Bar Rescue Will Have You Appalled
articles.summary: These are some wild stories I didn't expect.
articles.content:
Even the best reality TV shows can be accused of being scripted, and while not every claim is substantiated, there are a lot of allegations. Personally, like many others, I might be taken aback on the off chance that such a claim turns out to be true. Just recently, I found two stories from people who allegedly got a first-hand look at the inner workings of America's Got Talent and Bar Rescue , and they're fascinating to read.

It's not uncommon for reality TV show subjects to complain about receiving unflattering or dishonest edits. Over the years, stars have alleged that producers can get the response they want out of them and then edit the footage to make it appear they said something entirely different from what they meant. If AGT actually engaged in this, it wouldn't be different from claims against many other shows on the 2026 TV schedule . Regardless, this should be a gentle reminder for viewers not to believe everything they see.

From there, the writer claimed the bar's owners removed all the furniture and revamped the menu with new cocktails. His wife apparently stood in line to attend the reopening and was instructed before entering that she could only order the signature cocktail.

The whole account really makes me rethink the times I've seen Jon Taffer give advice on how to fix a bar . Of course, this is all alleged, and it's not like there are receipts or concrete proof of these claims. It isn't necessarily hard to believe, but given the lack of hard evidence or even any identifiable information, I'd take it with a grain of salt.

articles.title: From Venice Winner 'Woman Unknown' and Westeros to 'Star City': Meet Some of the Baltic Craft Specialists Who've Worked on Int'l Productions
articles.summary: The Baltic countries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are in focus at the 25th Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event market, part of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival.
articles.content:
Whether such Hollywood films as Christopher Nolan's Tenet , Venice 2026 winner Woman Unknown or such series as Paramount+ spy thriller The Agency , the BBC's War & Peace , and Apple TV's Star City – the Baltic countries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have been among the locations that international productions have turned to, bringing global audiences a look and taste of the region.

Film and TV craft experts have brought their skills to international and local crews alike.

With the 25th edition of the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event (ITBE) market, part of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF), currently shining a spotlight on the Baltic region, THR decided to check in with some creatives who have brought their talents to film and series you may well recognize. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Movies Dual Oscar Winner Christopher Hampton Calls Glenn Close Honorary Oscar "the Least They Can Do," Says AI Is Just "a Super Google" Music IVE, BINI, KiiiKiii, SB19, LiSA and Babymetal Score Grammy Nominations in New Asian Pop Category

Meet some of the faces you want to or should know below.

Ingrīda Nagle, location manager, Latvia You may have seen her work in: Woman Unknown (the first Latvian co-production in the main competition at Venice where it won the Golden Lion. The Latvian capital Riga is standing in for post-war Denmark); Gomorrah ; Oleg ; Dogs Don't Wear Pants .

How long have you been working in your field, and what first inspired you to do this kind of creative work? I have been working in the film industry since 2009. It was a very interesting and challenging turn of events in my life, and I got into the industry through a fortunate coincidence. I was invited to work as a Production Assistant (PA) on the international biographical television film The Courageous Heart of Irena Sendler , which was shot in Latvia. In this role, I had to prove my abilities and versatility, which I handled successfully throughout the project. I received great recommendations and, inspired by my colleagues, began focusing specifically on location management. Over the years, working on many different and challenging projects, I realized that I truly enjoy this work. As my skills developed, I found it increasingly rewarding. It is worth noting that before starting my career in film, I graduated from the Riga Film Studio Acting School, so in a way, working in cinema was already waiting for me. I am deeply grateful for this twist of fate, which fundamentally changed my professional career. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

What are some of the big international productions you have worked on? How did they find you and your skills, and how did they hire you? I have worked on a number of notable feature films and series. Among them are films such as Dogs Don't Wear Pants ; Oleg ; The Exalted ; Modris ; the series Gomorrah ; The Invisible Fight , and most recently, the award-winning feature Woman Unknown . For the most part, producers reach out to me based on recommendations regarding my ability to think out of the box, offer unconventional location ideas, as well as my multitasking abilities, communication skills, and professional attitude. In the film industry, accuracy, the ability to navigate complex situations, finding quick solutions, while maintaining creativity and a good sense of humor, are highly valued – and I believe I possess all of these qualities.

Do you focus on either local or international work now or how do you choose projects? Currently, I am working on several large-scale international projects. I am pleased to say that my professional capabilities and level of work have [earned] a high degree of trust. However, whenever time and capacity allow, I also really enjoy working with local, talented directors and on smaller-scale projects. In these projects, where the crew is compact and creative freedom is high, a special “film family” feeling is created, which brings immense satisfaction in being an important part of making the movie.

Do you have any tips for young people who want to work in your field? My main advice is: travel more around your country, keep your eyes open, walk, explore, and discover! Throughout my life, I have covered most distances on foot, and that is precisely how I have discovered truly wonderful and unique locations. Be open to challenges, read plenty of books to develop your communication skills. Don't be afraid to make mistakes! Learn to look at places you have walked by a hundred times with “fresh eyes,” look up, notice the details, and let your imagination run wild. And be prepared to work hard – this role truly demands it. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

What are you working on right now? Currently, I am working on three international projects, which, due to NDAs is not confirmed for publicity yet, but I am currently waiting for approval from the producers to name them.

Kaire Hendrikson, make-up designer and special effects make-up artist, Estonia You may have seen her work in: The Agency : Tenet ; Azrael ; Deliver Us ; The Swedish Torpedo ; The Missile ; and the international drama series Estonia .

How long have you been working in your field, and what first inspired you to do this kind of creative work? I've been doing films for 22 years now. I lived in Italy after high school for years, and when I came back, one time, I thought that if I found something interesting in Estonia, I'd stay here for a while. Then I found a job as an assistant in film production company, and I fell in love with these people and the lifestyle. Then came the makeup academy, and the rest is history. What are some of the big international productions you have worked on? How did they find you and your skills, and how did they hire you? The Agency , the Paramount+ TV series with Michael Fassbender – I was supervising makeup artist during the Estonian shooting period, doing the actors with my U.K. collegues. Tenet by Christopher Nolan – I took care of the extras in Estonian shooting period. Burial by Ben Parker – I was a makeup designer on this U.K. production. Undergods by Chino Moya was a great adventure in Serbia, shooting a U.K., Belgium, Holland, Estonian co-production. The Swedish Torpedo – I really loved designing this Swedish movie. They usually find me through Estonian producers. Do you focus on either local or international work now or how do you choose projects? For the last 15 years, I've mainly worked on international productions. If I'm designing the makeup for a film, the script has to be interesting to me in one way or another – great story, interesting period to recreate, challenging SFX makeup, exciting character creating or very inspiring film director. I just refuse to be away from home and my family for months if there's nothing that excites me about the project. When it's a big international production like Tenet , just being part of a team that size and seeing how makeup artists from around the world work is inspiring in itself! Do you have any tips for young people who want to work in your field? It's a lifestyle with a lot of traveling, a lot of new people all the time, a lot of not knowing what and where the be next project is going to be, a lot of uncertainty, a lot of quick adaption, a lot of team work. So basically you have to have a bit of a Gypsy soul in you to enjoy it. If this sounds exciting, go for it – all the rest is learnable! I love it! What are you working on right now? I'm recovering from this crazy year and enjoying the time with my family now! I am also prepping a Norwegian period movie based on real story about very brave/crazy woman – lots of super nice SFX makeup and very nice period to create! It's going to be a busy year as there are also other super interesting projects waiting for the final green light.

Jurgita Globytė, makeup designer, Lithuania You may have seen her work in: Stranger Things ; Vesper; Truth & Treason ; Star City . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

How long have you been working in your field, and what first inspired you to do this kind of creative work? I have been doing this work for about 20 years. Before that, I studied business management, but I did not feel it was right for me. Later, I decided to change direction and chose to study make-up for film and theater. After finishing my studies at the make-up academy, I entered the film industry quite naturally, through a recommendation. One of my teachers recommended me to a film make-up artist who was looking for assistants. That is how my journey began. If you are open to learning and quickly understand how working in film works, you have a good chance to find your place, learn more and later do your own creative work.

What are some of the big international productions you have worked on? How did they find you and your skills, and how did they hire you? When international productions come to Lithuania, local producers recommend us. There is often a selection process, and that is how they choose their teams. One of the most memorable and beautiful projects I worked on was the BBC series War & Peace . Do you focus on either local or international work now or how do you choose projects? I am very happy to work on local projects. When I have a choice, I prefer them. We are a small film community, and it is always a great joy to create something at home. Directors who know how I work, my skills and my style invite me to work with them. Do you have any tips for young people who want to work in your field? My advice to young people would be to stay curious, be dedicated and enjoy what you do. What are you working on right now? articles.title: Yoda Could Lend You a Hand, and This Piece of His Original Empire Strikes Back Puppet Makes It Possible
articles.summary: What do you do when your decisions directly result in the formation of the Galactic Empire and the most promising young Jedi becoming the galaxy's biggest threat? You ship off the a remote swamp planet and train his son to defeat him, of course! Master Yoda may be the old wise sage of the Jedi, […]
articles.content:
Considering that the original puppet, controlled and voiced by Frank Oz, was created in 1980 out of foam latex, it's not surprising that it has come apart over the decades. However, since we only saw his head and hands, it's safe to assume that there wasn't really a ‘body' connecting them, just his garb thrown over some wiring. That means this is one part of the holy trinity that makes up the old Jedi Master, with the others being his right hand and head. Unfortunately, you're not going to get any words of wisdom if you put them together, but this part of the original puppet is definitely a Grail for Star Wars fans. With the foam latex disintegrating over time, the hand is evidently dried up and cracked, but it comes with an acrylic display case for safety.

Similar to Luke's quest to fly to Dagobah and take tutelage from the old Jedi Master, you can bet the prop's new owner is pondering whether to track down the other parts and finally reunite them. While his right hand and head shouldn't be too tough to find, it's unlikely that the puppet's robes have survived after all the years. Still, the going price will surely skyrocket if they manage to unite them all once again. That being said, this particular hand is the one Yoda held his cane in, and you can still see some of the marks left by it on the inner side. Perhaps his right hand, which he famously used to retrieve Luke Skywalker's X-Wing from the swamp may be a tad bit more valuable.

There's something a bit strange about collecting literal body parts of a beloved Star Wars characters, but I doubt that George Lucas and gang ever imagined during production that one part of the puppet would ever go for $15,000. While that's a massive price, it's almost nothing compared to some of the other original Star Wars props that recently sold on Heritage. Darth Vader's original lightsaber just sold for $5 million , while Luke Skywalker's went for for almost $4 million . More surprising is the fact that C-3POs prop glove went for more money than Yoda's hand, at $17,500. That almost makes this prop a steal by comparison. Prices aside, there's no doubt about the significance of this original prop from arguably the best Star Wars mainline movie.

Is Yoda the best Jedi Master in the Star Wars universe? Let us know in the comments!

articles.title: Only 1 Star Wars Actor Has Won an Emmy For Their Franchise Role, And It's Not Who You Think
articles.summary: The highly-decorated Star Wars saga has earned billions of dollars internationally with little left to accomplish as far as awards and prestige. However, within the franchise itself only one performer has won an Emmy — the awards honoring the television industry — and it couldn't have gone to a more fitting person. David Tennant crossed […]
articles.content:
Tennant won the award in 2013, and in the nearly 15 years since that happened, no other performer in a Star Wars show has claimed it again. Other series have been nominated and won awards, yet somehow their actors keep getting snubbed. It's a rare feather in the cap for Tennant, one that he has the singular distinction of holding across the enormous Star Wars universe to this day. But to many fans who know him from a different sci-fi series, his Clone Wars role would be the last thing they would associate with him when it comes to winning awards.

During the 40th annual Daytime Entertainment Emmy Awards in 2013, Tennant took home the award for Outstanding Performer in an Animated Program thanks to his voice acting in Star Wars: Clone Wars . Tennant's portrayal of the Mark IV architect droid professor in the episodes “A Test of Strength” and “A Necessary Bond,” which were two pieces of a larger four-parter that centered around a group of young Padawans enduring a ritual Jedi rite of passage that goes awry during the show's fifth and final season. Jim Cummings and Sam Witwer, who respectively played Hondo Ohnaka and Darth Maul in the show, were also nominated in the same category alongside Tennant.

On that same night, Clone Wars also won Outstanding Special Class Animated Program, with Star Wars: The Clone Wars creator and executive producer George Lucas accepting. The queen herself, Carrie Fisher, presented the award and was visibly excited to make the announcement. This was not too long after Lucas completed the sale of the franchise to Disney at the end of 2012, and its future was still uncertain with how the House of Mouse would handle it, so the timing of this award for many fans was very important. The final season of Clone Wars was also nominated in three other categories — Outstanding Directing in an Animated Program, Outstanding Achievement in Sound Mixing – Animation and Outstanding Achievement in Music Direction and Composition — but those awards went to other programs.

Tennant is likely one of the only performers to win the Daytime Emmy, a Scottish BAFTA and a Welsh BAFTA, thought he has yet to earn a British BAFTA. It turns out he is also a massive Star Wars fan, and has been one for as long as he can remember. “Probably the first film i really remember getting obsessed with was the original Star Wars ,” Tennant, who was six at the time Episode IV came out, said in his 2024 interview with BAFTA. “ Star Wars was a film that wasn't necessarily expected to become a global phenomenon that it did… And we went to see [it] and it was extraordinary! Mind-bending, like nothing I'd ever seen before. And I became very obsessed with Star Wars from that moment on to this day, probably.”

After the animated Clone Wars , Tennant revived the ancient Jedi training droid in Disney+'s live-action Ahsoka Tano series in 2023. The show's long-awaited second season returns to the streaming service in early 2027, and according to a trailer shown at this summer's past D23 event, Huyang is expected to return with Tennant once again providing his voice. The producers, cast and crew have all agreed that working with Tennant has been a dream come true, and the fans have felt the same way. Think about it – how often do you get a time-traveling doctor, an immortal demon, Scrooge McDuck and a multi-armed droid who can build a lightsaber all in the same room? By hiring David Tennant.

With Ahsoka Tano's second season only a few more months away, what are you hoping to see when the series returns? Join the conversation in the comments below.

articles.title: Niv Fichman’s Rhombus Media Sells to Skywild Pictures (Exclusive)
articles.summary: The ‘Blackberry’ and 'The Sympathizer' producer will stay on with the enlarged indie Canadian producer led by Angela Jennings after a nearly-50 year career shaping Canadian cinema.
articles.content:
Rhombus Media founder and producer Niv Fichman has announced the sale of the indie banner he launched in 1979 to Angela Jennings' Skywild Pictures as her new indie outfit scales up in film and TV production.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but Fichman, who produced Matt Johnson's Blackberry and Park Chan-wook's The Sympathizer miniseries for HBO Max, will remain with Skywild as lead producer. "It's coming on 50 years soon," Fichman told The Hollywood Reporter about his role in shaping Canadian cinema for nearly five decades as a maestro of complex international co-productions, and with credits for over 200 feature films and television projects.

The acquisition will see Skywild combine its mostly TV development team with Fichman's established film producers team – including senior producers Fraser Ash as senior vp of content and Kevin Krikst as vp of production — and with Rhombus operating as a semi-autonomous label under the Skywild banner to maintain its brand identity.

Fichman, 70, added about the rationale for the sales deal: "They have an identical artistic vision to what we have, which is to produce high quality Canadian content shows to take to the world and work with the greatest artists and actors, television showrunners and people like that, which we've done.” For her part, Jennings goes from president to CEO of the enlarged company after launching Skywild in 2025 with Travis Farncombe, who becomes executive chair after serving as CEO.

"He (Fichman) wasn't looking hard to sell, and we weren't looking hard to buy. But when the discussions got underway, we realized what a hand and glove fit we had for both companies," Jennings said of matching her business expertise with the creative brain trust at Rhombus. Skywild's leadership team includes Natalie Urquhart as vp of content and Olivia Tharme as director of development.

Tying up with Skywild marks a new chapter for Rhombus, where Fichman over nearly a half-century became known for knitting together international co-productions to share the financing and risk on producing auteur-driven films and TV series. These include Denis Villeneuve's Enemy, starring Jake Gyllenhaal, Francois Girard's The Red Violin, which earned the 2000 Oscar winner for best original score, Atom Egoyan's The Seven Veils, Brandon Cronenberg's Possessor, Fernando Meirelles' Blindness , starring Julianne Moore and Mark Ruffalo, and Patricia Rozema's Into the Forest.

Fichman more recently executive produced the Noomi Rapace-starring cat-and-mouse thriller In Alaska , which premiered in Toronto. His Rhombus Media titles have become mainstays of major film festivals, including Cannes, Sundance, Berlin and Venice. Fichman's other TV credits include Andrew Haigh's The North Water, a co-production with See-Saw Films that starred Colin Farrell and Jack O'Connell and was acquired by BBC Two and AMC+.

Upcoming Rhombus projects include two feature films in production: Child's Play, a Canada-UK co-production starring Sandra Oh and directed by China's Wang XiaoShuai, and an untitled Matt Johnson film starring Finn Wolfhard.

Skywild's next chapter follows the new company having assembled a development slate of more than a dozen projects, both original and based on foundational IP. Those projects include optioning popular YA novel writer Tom Ryan's first adult murder mystery, The Treasure Hunters Club , for a TV adaptation, and two other novels for its TV series development slate: the thriller Our Little Secret by Edward Kay and Mikhael Klassen-Kay, and The Affinities by Hugo Award–winning author Robert Charles Wilson.

Jennings argued expanding Skywild via an acquisition during a time of unprecedented industry change made sense for her, especially as the Canadian federal government in Ottawa increases its investment in homegrown film and TV content for export worldwide. "It's never been better to be Canadian, and our goal is ambitious and falls onto what Niv has already done for nearly 50 years, which is deliver the highest level Canadian content to the world," she said.

After producing Park Chan-wook's The Sympathizer miniseries as a co-production with A24, Fichman has been at work structuring around six Korean projects as co-productions, to be shot mostly in Canada. That follows Canada and South Korea in April 2026 signing an updated international co-production treaty to make it easier for filmmakers and other creators from both countries to work together.

For Fichman, who has long been an ambassador for Canadian co-productions with international partners, the latest push for multi-passport films and TV series is part of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's post-Davos mission to have Canada coordinate with so-called middle powers to diversify from a business and trade reliance on the U.S. market.

"I've been very careful when going abroad to promote co-productions that are specific to my own. And with respect to the U.S., we are aligning ourselves with other places and, frankly, the U.S. companies really love those productions that we're working on," Fichman insisted. The pivot to a South Korea where that country's cinema is succeeding across a range of genres also comes as the economics of U.S. indie moviemaking is in flux, and Canadian indie producers are tapping other foreign partners for bigger budgets to penetrate world markets.

Back on the home front, Rhombus is at work on new films from directors Mathieu Denis, Louise Archambault, Jeff Lemire and Brandon Cronenberg, and a TV series from Kim Cattrall and Don McKellar.

EXCLUSIVE: Netflix has ordered a second season of Polish drama Anaesthesia ( Znieczulenie ).

The medical drama was a hit for the streamer, hitting the Top 10 list in Poland almost immediately after it launched and remaining there to this day, and is also fifth on Netflix's global chart. Little surprise Season 2 has been greenlit in that context.

"We have a pretty exciting year ahead of us," said producer Philipp Goeser.

"It's a wide array of topics and styles, but at the core are handpicked stories that are very authentic and personal. We're always looking for authentic new voices and stories. Most of our [upcoming] titles are debut films, which is a very important focus for the company."

This includes elevated thriller " The Matriarch ," which will have its world premiere at the 30th Black Nights Film Festival. Sold by Pluto Film, it'll be distributed in Germany by Four Guys Film Distribution.

The film follows 17-year-old Kim, who enters her mother's trafficking business. They bring Vietnamese migrants to Europe and, predictably, others want a piece of the pie as well.

"We work very closely with the artists. We want to support their vision and ‘The Matriarch' is a perfect example of that," said Goeser.

It's the first film with an almost exclusively Vietnamese-German cast, one that features Tuyen Do, Viet Pham, Trang Le Hong, Lissy-Marie Nguyen, Viet Long Hoang and Marlon Minh-Hai Leyck. "Our projects are arthouse, but they also have a commercial side. Alison and I discussed that very early on. How can we tell an edgy family drama about a mother and a daughter and also give it a genre twist?"

Kuhn agreed: "Personally, I wish arthouse and mainstream cinema would find their way back to each other rather than drifting further and further apart. As someone who directs both commercial streaming series and auteur-driven, personal films, I'd love for us to rediscover the magical sweet spot that existed in cinema before the turn of the millennium."

Growing up as a biracial German-Vietnamese child, she only saw people on screen who resembled one half of her family.

"Having had the privilege of studying directing at a prestigious film school, I wanted to use my position behind the camera to create complex, breathing protagonists of Vietnamese descent who aren't the nerdy overachiever providing comic relief or the waitress who appears in just one scene, speaking with a stereotypical accent," she said.

Kuhn wanted to bring a different perspective to the table and to look at her protagonists with empathy.

"To me, empathy is probably the most important word in filmmaking. I want to understand what drives my main characters to make certain choices, even when those choices might be morally questionable," she noted.

"Although the film is told from the daughter's perspective, it was important to understand the mother as well. As a woman in the diaspora who has never been accepted as an equal by German society, she has achieved an incredible amount through sheer determination. She has built a system that provides stability for her family in Vietnam and her children in Germany, but it comes at an enormous cost to her."

In the film, the mother wants to protect her daughter from that life but ultimately has to accept her help.

"The daughter, Kim, is our emotional anchor throughout the story. She experiences things that anyone who has ever been a teenager can relate to: curiosity about the world, the discovery of romance and sexuality, the desire to experiment and find her own identity."

In a way, though, Kim can also be seen as a reflection of her mother's younger self, forced to sacrifice her personal desires. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"My hope is that audiences will feel the love between mother and daughter and root for them to find their way to each other."

“The Matriarch” is produced by Martin Lehwald, Goeser and Marcos Kantis, while Paula Elina Klossner and Stephan Buske co-produce.

"Anatol," sold by Beta Cinema, will be a lighter proposition. It shows a boy who, after studying philosophy, finds himself on a job-hunting odyssey full of quirky encounters, family rivalries, white lies and mishaps.

"It's a tragicomedy with an arthouse story," said Goeser, comparing the film to the works of Joachim Trier. "The script is amazing and it's really, really funny."

Filming will begin in January, with Alamode set to distribute in Germany.

"The Good German" is a historical drama about Duala Manga Bell, the German-educated Cameroonian king who fought the colonial seizure of Duala land through the courts. He was executed after a sham trial in 1914.

Beside him – yet ultimately against him – is Hermann Röhm, a childhood acquaintance turned colonial official.

Other new projects include "Ruki's First Summer" and TV series "Nuclear Sunset Cruise," both inspired by true events yet completely different.

"It's a sweet tale of growing up between two worlds. It's a very European topic. Amidst all the negativity surrounding migration, we wanted to demonstrate how children can sometimes solve problems that we, as a society, have been unable to," noted Goeser.

"Nuclear Sunset Cruise," overseen by writer-director Florian Gallenberger and set at the height of the Cuban Missile Crisis in October 1962, focuses on an East German cruise ship that sails unknowingly into the U.S. naval blockade while en route to Havana.

"We decided to make it a comedy, and it ended up being like ‘The White Lotus.' Disney ‘s years-long effort to unify the Disney+ and Hulu apps is “nearly complete,” Mouse House execs said, as the company looks to concentrate its streaming firepower on the Disney+ platform.

The company made the announcement in reporting earnings for the September 2026 quarter .

Beginning this December, Disney+ and Hulu bundle subscribers “will have a fully unified experience on Disney+, including live TV and select premium add-ons, creating a more seamless way to discover and engage with the breadth of content across our brands and franchises,” CEO Josh D'Amaro and CFO Hugh Johnston said in their quarterly letter to shareholders. “We believe our continued focus on product and technology will yield further benefits in engagement and churn over time.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Former NCT Member Lucas Wong Makes Acting Debut in Taiwanese Folk-Music Drama 'A Time' With Jerry Yan, Ning Chang at Taiwan Creative Content Fest 'African Kung-Fu Nazis' Franchise Lands at Hong Kong’s Cappu Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE)

Also in December, Disney expects to begin introducing creator content on Disney+ through its recent agreement with TikTok . The TikTok content rollout will be “strategically aligned” to the lead-up to Marvel's “Avengers: Doomsday” theatrical premiere on Dec. 18, according to the Disney execs.

“We are also adding more vertical video, live sports and podcasts to the [Disney+] platform, while continuing to explore other emerging content genres,” D'Amaro and Johnston said.

Disney's integration of Hulu and Disney+ kicked off in 2023 under then-CEO Bob Iger , two years before the company closed its deal with Comcast to buy out NBCUniversal‘s one-third stake in Hulu in June 2025.

This September, Disney announced another round of streaming price hikes , its fourth rate increases in as many years. The pricing strategy is aimed at pushing consumers toward bundles: The Disney+/Hulu Premium bundle increased two dollars, from $19.99 to $21.99/month, which is nearly half what it costs if you purchase them separately, while the ad-supported Disney+/Hulu bundle remained unchanged at $12.99/month (just 50 cents more than each of the services purchased individually).

According to Disney's D'Amaro and Johnston, ESPN “plays an important role in the overall Disney portfolio by contributing live and on-demand offerings to Disney+, lifting engagement and supporting revenue growth, and encouraging users to upgrade to the Disney+, Hulu, ESPN bundle.”

articles.content:
Disney had a robust quarter, topping Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines. But CEO Josh D'Amaro, who's been in the job for eight months, sees an opportunity for the company to become even more efficient and help fuel future growth.

For the three months ended Oct. 3, 2026, which is Disney's fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, the Mouse House reported revenue of $25.95 billion, up 16%, and a doubling of net income to $2.61 billion. Total operating segment income rose 43%, to $4.97 billion. The company reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.77. On average, Wall Street analysts expected revenue of $25.16 billion and adjusted earnings of $1.68 per share, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘Kamen Rider' Studio Toei Frames Generative AI Rules, Sets First Video Games for 2027 'Lord of the Rings,' 'Avatar' VFX House Weta FX Partners With Taiwan’s Moonshine Studio Under AI Pact With TAICCA

Overall, it was a solid quarter across Disney's entertainment, sports and theme parks businesses. But D'Amaro and his lieutenants are looking to make Disney leaner and meaner. “We now expect the program to realize annual run-rate operating expense savings of about $3 billion by fiscal 2029,” the execs wrote. “While these efficiencies will be used primarily to fund future growth, we do expect a portion to drop to the bottom line over time.” Disney is poised to make a significant round of layoffs in the current quarter, affecting thousands of employees, with some managers reportedly told to cut expenses by 20% on an annualized basis . blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

In addition, the execs said, they expect cash content spending in fiscal 2027 of approximately $26 billion, up about 9% from fiscal 2026. That includes “our increased investment in international programming and sports rights, and the timing of feature film production spend,” D'Amaro and Johnston said.

Disney noted that its fourth quarter and fiscal 2026 results had one additional week of operations (a 53rd week) compared with the year-earlier period. The company estimates that the 53rd week contributed approximately 17 cents to full-year adjusted earnings per share.

Revenue from Disney+ and Hulu rose 22% to $5.13 billion in the September 2026 quarter, and operating income more than doubled to $824 million. Disney said it expects to complete the integration of Disney+ and Hulu before the end of 2026 , with a “fully unified experience” available in December.

Starting with the December 2026 quarter, Disney will stop reporting operating income for Disney+ and Hulu. “We have made strong progress scaling our SVOD businesses and, as a result, see a long runway for growth and margin expansion at Disney Entertainment,” D'Amaro and Johnston wrote in the letter. “We no longer believe the supplemental disclosure of SVOD operating income reflects this segment focus and strategy.”

In another financial reporting change, Disney as of Q1 of fiscal 2027 will provide additional revenue disclosures for Disney Entertainment, to “provide greater visibility into how we monetize Entertainment content across distribution platforms, third-party licensing and consumer products,” the company's execs said.

In the September quarter, Disney's Entertainment segment overall saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income in the segment shot up 92% to $1.33 billion “due to growth in subscription and affiliate fees and higher content sales, partially offset by increased programming and production costs.”

The execs touted the company's intellectual-property flywheel between theatrical and streaming movie releases. Disney-Pixar's “Toy Story 5,” which raked in $1.15 billion globally at the box office this summer, premiered on Disney+ on Sept. 23, and garnered 20 million views in its first five days on the platform. According to Disney, August was the highest month ever for Marvel Studios viewing, fueled by the summer theatrical success of “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” (released by Sony Pictures) and the debut of the “Avengers: Doomsday trailer.” During the quarter, Marvel content viewership on Disney+ more than doubled compared with its historical baseline. “Our successful rerelease of ‘Avengers: Endgame' in late September also showed how anticipation continues to build for ‘Avengers: Doomsday,' which arrives in theaters December 18,” D'Amaro and Johnston said in the letter. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

At ESPN, revenue increased 16% to $4.61 billion. Growth in subscription and affiliate fees came from an increase of 8% from the additional week of operations in the quarter compared with the year-earlier period, 6% from higher rates and 4% from Disney's deal with the NFL giving the league a 10% ownership stake in ESPN.

Disney Experiences revenue hit $10.11 billion in the September quarter, up 15%, with 5% of the growth in theme park admissions sales coming from higher average per capita ticket revenue. Segment operating income increased 20% to $2.25 billion. Disney Experiences saw an 11% increase in global visitors in the quarter (or a 4% increase excluding the 53rd week). “We continued to see headwinds from lower international attendance at our domestic parks in the quarter, but as expected, those headwinds moderated from the year-over-year impact observed in the third quarter,” D'Amaro and Johnston said.

For fiscal 2027, Disney is expecting double-digit growth in adjusted EPS (excluding the impact of the 53rd week in '26). Disney expects the majority of its growth in total segment operating income and adjusted EPS for fiscal 2027 to occur in the first half of the fiscal year.

In fiscal '27, Disney expects capital expenditures of approximately $9 billion “as we continue to execute against our strategy to turbocharge growth at Disney Experiences,” the execs said. The company invested $8.7 billion parks, resorts and other property in the 2026 fiscal year.

In August, Disney closed the sale of its 50% stake in A+E Global Media to co-owner Hearst for $1.2 billion in cash. For fiscal 2026, A+E contributed approximately $390 million in equity income to Disney's Entertainment segment operating income.

Also Tuesday, Disney's board declared a cash dividend of $2.00 per share payable over the course of fiscal 2027, a 33% increase over the $1.50 per share paid to shareholders during fiscal year 2026.

articles.title: Christopher Hampton on AI – ‘I’m More Interested in Real Intelligence'– and Dos and Don’t’s of Screenwriting
articles.summary: “The least they could do,” Sir Christopher Hampton said about Glenn Close’s Honorary Oscar at the Tallinn Film Festival where at a masterclass, “From Stage to Screen, The Art of Adaptation,” the two-time Oscar winner delivered sometimes trenchant takes on AI – ‘I’m more interested in real intelligence' – and how screenwriting was like gambling […]
articles.content:
"The least they could do," Sir Christopher Hampton said about Glenn Close 's Honorary Oscar at the Tallinn Film Festival where at a masterclass, "From Stage to Screen, The Art of Adaptation," the two-time Oscar winner delivered sometimes trenchant takes on AI – ‘I'm more interested in real intelligence' – and how screenwriting was like gambling at a casino.

"It's about time!," Hampton said of Close's Honorary Oscar."I was very happy to hear that. I think she's still hoping to get one for acting in a specific role, but that hasn't happened yet, so the least they could do was giving her an Honorary Oscar, I guess" blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'African Kung-Fu Nazis' Franchise Lands at Hong Kong’s Cappu Films for International Sales (EXCLUSIVE) Alien Cat Sent to Conquer Earth Goes Soft for Catnip and Canned Tuna in Taiwan Creative Content Fest Animated Series 'Operation Maomao'

Unpacking a list of dos and don'ts for screenwriting, using AI was definitely not on the to-do side. In fact, he couldn't care less about the topic.

Comparing AI to "a sort of super Google," Hampton said "AI hasn't troubled me very much. I'm more interested in real intelligence, and I think the flaw in artificial intelligence is in the name because it's artificial."

Asked whether he thought AI could replace screenwriters he said: "I don't think it's gonna happen, as ‘our ‘work is more interesting than ‘its' work." And for those newcomers tempted by writing a script with the help of AI he said: "You're being lazy by allowing some other some other external force to take over you; you might as well choose a different profession."

In fact, at the opening session of the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event's training program Discovery Campus, Hampton who is also juror at the festival's official selection, warned newcomers about the hardships of screenwriting and of works actually landing on screens. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"Writing for film is really like going into the casino, he said. "You sit at the table, you put your money under 20 and the chances of the film being made the way you imagined are so tiny that when it does happen, it's incredibly, incredibly fulfilling and it gives you an enormous amount of pleasure. But most of the time, the croupier just takes the chips away and that's it!!"

He said aspiring scribes should accept the fact that "there's a lot of wastage in writing. A lot of projects that you will spend six, nine months or a year writing, will never be seen in any form because somehow, they haven't been financed."

Numerous of his works have never been filmed, he admitted, despite his stellar career as playwright, screenwriter, translator and director spanning five decades that earned him multiple nods and a knighthood for services to drama,

Hampton mentioned an adaptation of the life of Dmitri Shostakovich, "his struggles as a composer in the Soviet Union," written three-four years ago. "I haven't been able to get it made because people don't want to engage with or don't want to make a film about Russia, set in Russia, dealing with Russians. I find it paradoxical because of course it's just the time when it would be interesting to see a film about a man who struggled his whole life with the political system and somehow found ways to circumvent all the roadblocks that were put in his way," he added.

Similarly, another project set in Indonesia in the 1950s, against the background of a conflict between fundamentalist and moderate Muslims, was rejected by financiers due to the topic viewed as problematic at the time, just post 09/11.

He also underscored that many of his works have taken years – sometimes decades – to turn into features. "My projects are very, very slow," he acknowledged, citing David Cronenberg's "A Dangerous Method" that took 14 years, and his directorial debut "Carrington" (a double winner at Cannes 1995) 18 years from script to screen. As for the anticipated "Embers" starring Ralph Fiennes and Viggo Mortensen, Hampton said the screen adaptation of Sándor Márais's acclaimed novel, lined up for 2027, has been 20 years in the making. "I finally got it made with the director I wanted, the great Hungarian director István Szabó," he said. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"You just have to be patient!" advised Hampton who still hopes that some films that have been waiting 30-40 years might still be picked up, such as the David Lean adaptation of Joseph Conrad's 1904 novel "Nostromo," which was shelved partly due to the director's failing health and eventual death in 1991.

Unpacking the art of screenwriting, Hampton said Lean, the Oscar-winning British director of "Lawrence of Arabia "was together with the legendary Fred Zinneman ("High Noon," "From Here to Eternity") two filmmakers who had determining influences on him.

Having started in 1973 with the adaptation of Ibsen's "A Doll's House," starring Anthony Hopkins, he said it took him more than a decade to fully grasp the difference between writing for theatre – something that came easily to him – and writing for film. "I didn't realise that moving from a stage play to a film was more than simply repeating the dialogue in front of a camera. And it took me about 10 years to figure out how not to make a film from a play which smelt like the theatre."

The mistake he made was thinking that it was easier to write films than theatre plays, he reckoned. "In other words, you think a film gives you enormous liberty, you can jump from London to Hong Kong in one cut, but that liberty imposes on you a number of constraints that I hadn't been aware of before," he said.

From working with Lean, he learned "how to make a scene flow into another, even if it's in a different location or a different subject," and he learned to respect "a film's cohesion, although it might be cut into several chapters like a novel.

From working nine months with Fred Zinnemann ("High Noon," From Here to Eternity") on a project about the last days of WWII – eventually cancelled following a change of boss at 20th Century Fox, he learned to focus on "telling the story, just the story."

After his collaboration with Lean and Zinnemann, Hampton said he went straight to working on Stephen Frears' " Dangerous Liaisons ." "For the first time after 10-15 years of writing screenplays, I felt like I kind of knew what I was doing."

Cronenberg was another visionary filmmaker who had an impact on him and from whom he picked up how to be "more economical," something he then applied for instance while writing the first draft of Florian Zeller's "The Son (2022). "The first thing I did was cut 20 pages!" said the screenwriter who insisted on keeping a story to its core. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"One of the most important skills that you can achieve as a screenwriter is to know what you need to say and don't say any more than that. It's really a question of defining what's essential," he noted.

Expanding on the subject, he said that some filmmakers unnecessarily, feel the urge to over-explain, underestimating the audience "who is always more intelligent than people imagine." He said U.S. Studios with their numerous notes, often ask him "to explain this or that," things that "are there in the script already that they haven't noticed."

Hampton went on criticising Hollywood's formula filmmaking, blockbusters based on universes, that "actually I find completely incomprehensible," he admitted. He also pointed at the U.S. studios' aversion for ‘original' works. He said during a test-screening of his 2003 "Imagining Argentina," one of three works he directed, when a young member of the audience described the film as being original "the [studio] executive next to me put his face in his hands and groaned because there's nothing more difficult for them than something that's original."

Similarly, Hampton dismissed today's TV drama, after being asked by Variety if he was tempted by the format. Unlike in the 1970s, when he would write "a lot" for the BBC when they would produce two to three TV plays and films a week, he said he wasn't tempted by what he calls "a brutal medium" today. The last series he worked on was "The Singapore Grip" which aired on ITV in 2020.

"It took me such a long time, and there were so many notes to negotiate from the people making it. I just thought television really wasn't worth it anymore," he said. While acknowledging that television "provides an enormous amount of work for writers" today, he described the form as probably "the most constricted, prescriptive and unimaginative." "I don't really understand why the freedom that we used to have when I was young – and was very lucky to have –~ no longer exists," he stated.

articles.title: 3 Fantasy Movies That Were Too Ambitious For Their Own Good (& Suffered For It)
articles.summary: Humans have been telling fantasy stories since long before movies even existed, but the big screen has given us a platform to do so better than ever. Many of the best fantasy movies have indelibly imprinted themselves on our collective pop culture consciousness, with their stories and characters becoming beloved in their own right. As […]
articles.content:
Across the history of the genre, many fantasy movies have been punished for trying too much too soon. Filling a fantasy movie with attempts to build a wider mythos prematurely can go against it, as can attempting to establish a world much bigger than the movie's story necessarily warrants. While that sort of ambition deserves to be celebrated, if it comes at the detriment of the movie in question, then it tends to backfire pretty spectacularly.

Guy Ritchie's many career successes made the announcement of his adaptation of classic Arthurian legend seem especially exciting. With Charlie Hunnam cast as the hero King Arthur, the movie seemed to have the potential to be a true fantasy epic. This could easily have been an amazing fantasy movie , but a few creative missteps ruined its chances. Ritchie leaned into his familiar crutch of using English gangster-movie dialogue, and filled the film with visual-effects-heavy action sequences that tried to establish it as the entry point to a new world of supernatural fantasy. This might have even worked, had it not been marketed as an adaptation of the familiar legend of King Arthur, which meant it also needed to establish the many key figures and ideas associated with the legend alongside its original fantasy ideas. Trying to balance it all in a single movie simply didn't work, affecting the film's pacing and ultimately contributing to its poor reception.

2007's The Golden Compass can be best described as a forgotten fantasy movie that tried to start a franchise and failed miserably. Based on the first novel in Philip Pullman's complex His Dark Materials fantasy trilogy, Northern Lights , The Golden Compass attempted to establish the huge scope of the story in its opening chapter. Introducing parallel universes, religious authoritarianism, and mysterious scientific phenomena as part of its story all in the first movie was a lot, and it killed any chance of a franchise before it ever even got itself going. Trying to bring the entirety of Northern Lights to life on the screen simply felt like a jumbled mess, and the one thing that the movie sacrificed was the source material's controversial religious themes, which ironically was perhaps the worst thing to leave out. The result was a movie that tried to do far too much all at once, but also robbed itself of the main source of narrative depth in the novel.

Mortal Engines is perhaps best characterized as science fantasy, but it's another movie that was too ambitious for its own good. The fantasy movie from the 2010s adapted Philip Reeve's novel of the same name, a task which in itself was hugely ambitious. Telling the story of colossal mobile cities that hunt and consume smaller settlements was never going to be an easy thing to accomplish, and the 2018 movie couldn't quite pull it off. While Mortal Engines succeeded in bringing many key aspects of the original story to life on the big screen, so much attention was given to fitting everything in that the film's central adventure felt dull and formulaic, and its characters seemed underdeveloped. It seemed designed to set up a franchise of movies, but in the pursuit of this ambition, Mortal Engines forgot that the first film needed to be successful in order to get audiences invested. In that regard, the movie's ambitious nature served only to work against it, killing the planned franchise before it even began.

"But as soon as I walked in, they asked, How are you with blood? They then gave me a hat and scrubs, and I went in," Findlay recalls. What Findlay saw that day informs part of her next feature, Do No Harm .

The film follows Anna, a young doctor, who accepts a voluntary night shift away from her family on Christmas Eve. When her mentor, Dr. Petersen, is called away, Anna is left in charge of an overstretched maternity ward. With the pressure mounting, she has to make a series of urgent, critical decisions way beyond her experience. Just as things seem to be under control, Anna realises she's made a tiny and very human error that may end up costing a patient her life.

Findlay says the experience of giving birth to her son initially sparked the idea to explore a story set in the world of healthcare.

"I felt the experience was as close to being in a thriller as I could have imagined," she says. "It's like being on a train that was impossible to get off. There was a sense of being in a relentless present tense, with no way out of the experience except through it."

Findlay cites Sebastian Schipper 2015 feature Victoria as a thematic inspiration, but says the project fits into a substantial gap in the market she has identified around the representations of childbirth in contemporary filmmaking.

"I felt there weren't many representations of labour and childbirth that really spoke to that visceral, thriller-like feeling," she says. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"So often, the images we see of childbirth and labour are essentially cozy. Often they're from a male perspective: you can run through the familiar images in your head, like somebody's waters breaking in a supermarket. I'd never seen anything that captured the sense of it as a reckoning with mortality."

Findlay is best known in international film circles for her debut feature Midwinter Break (2026), written by Nick Payne, and starring Lesley Manville and Ciarán Hinds. The feature premiered at the Glasgow Film Festival before a theatrical release via Focus Features. However, Findlay is also one of the UK's most prolific theatre directors. Her recent productions include Alma Mater (Almeida Theatre); White Noise, A Number (The Bridge); Rutherford & Son, Beginning and Middle (National Theatre), and The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie (Donmar).

Do No Harm will mark the first time Findlay has directed a feature from a screenplay she has also written.

"I started writing to work out what the idea was, and as I kept writing, it acquired its own momentum and became something I felt able to write," Findlay says of the process.

"I'd always wanted to write something, and I've spent a lot of time in the theatre working on new writing. I suppose that, over time working in theatre, I'd built up a kind of toolkit by osmosis."

Findlay says she has "two really brilliant actors" attached to play Anna and Dr. Petersen, but cannot yet disclose who they are. Financing is still underway.

"We're hoping to shoot next year," she says. "The BBC has been behind the project from the very beginning. It's BBC Films, Fable and Hinterland Productions, and MK2 is doing the sales for us."

Findlay added: "We've got a really great team and a lot of pre-sales happening, so I think it will happen."
